opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think this is one of those places where it really helps to go back to Wittgenstein, because the way the question is usually framed already carries a lot of philosophical baggage. The picture we're tempted by is that when you and I both look at a ripe tomato, each of us has a little inner object, a private "red" sensation, and the word "red" is a label we attach to it. The worry then is: how could I ever know that your inner object is the same as mine? Maybe your red is my green, and we'd never find out.

What Wittgenstein shows, especially in the private language argument and the beetle-in-the-box passage, is that if the meaning of "red" really depended on some essentially private item, that item would drop out of the language game altogether. Everyone has a box with something in it they call a "beetle," nobody can look into anyone else's box, and yet the word works perfectly well in our shared practice. So whatever is in the box, it isn't doing the work of fixing the meaning. The meaning lives in the public practice: pointing at things, agreeing that the traffic light is red, correcting a child who calls an orange thing red, painting, matching swatches, and so on.

I want to be careful, though, because people sometimes hear that as a denial that there's anything going on inside, as if it were crude behaviourism. That's not the point. Of course I see red, and of course there's something it's like for me. The point is more subtle. Our concept of experience, our very talk about "what it's like," is itself rooted in a shared public world. The inner isn't a hidden realm that the words point into from outside. It's something that shows up in how we live together, how we respond to one another, what we can share and discuss.

So when two people talk about seeing red, I'd say they aren't trying to compare two hidden objects and failing. They're succeeding at something perfectly real: they're participating in a common practice that's grounded in a common world. The sceptical question, "but is your red really like my red?", starts to look less like a deep unanswerable question and more like a case of language idling, a question that has lost contact with the practices that give it sense.

And this matters a lot for the questions we'll probably get to about AI. If we think of consciousness as an essentially private inner light, then asking whether some exotic entity, a large language model or a robot, is conscious becomes a metaphysical mystery with no foothold at all. But if we take the Wittgensteinian view seriously, then the question is partly about whether we could come to treat that entity as a fellow participant in our shared world, whether our language of experience could naturally extend to it through engaging with it. That's not a cheap answer, and it doesn't make the hard questions disappear, but it puts them somewhere we can actually work with them.

r001.rationale: The response says that people successfully participate in a common public practice when they talk about seeing red, grounded in shared ways of identifying and discussing red things.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I'm quite suspicious of the way that distinction gets set up in the first place. The standard picture is that there's the public world of behaviour and brains and words, and then there's this private inner theatre where the red actually shows up, and you have access to yours and I have access to mine, and the great puzzle is how we could ever know whether your red is like my red. And I think that picture, which is a very natural one, is deeply misleading. It's the sort of thing Wittgenstein was getting at with the private language argument and the beetle in the box.

So the thought there is that if I say "red" and you say "red", and we both point at the same ripe tomato, and we both stop at the same traffic lights, and we agree about which paint chips match, then the word is doing its job. It's doing all the work it needs to do in the public domain. And if there were some further private thing, the beetle in each of our boxes, that nobody else could ever look at, then it would drop out of the language game altogether. It couldn't be what the word refers to, because nothing about how we use the word depends on it. As Wittgenstein says, the box might even be empty.

Now people hear that and they think I'm denying that there's anything it's like to see red, that I'm some kind of eliminativist. And I'm not. Of course when I look at a red thing there's an experience there. What I'm resisting is the move from "there is an experience" to "there is a private object that I'm inwardly inspecting, which is fundamentally hidden from you". That extra metaphysical step is where the trouble starts. Once you take it, you've generated the hard problem, you've generated the inverted spectrum, you've generated zombies, and you've made it a mystery how we ever talk about experience at all. Whereas in fact we talk about it perfectly well, all the time, in a shared language that we learned from each other.

So my view is that the concept of experience, including the concept of seeing red, is a public concept through and through. It's rooted in our shared lives, in our shared embodiment, in the fact that we're the same kind of creature responding to the same kind of world. The "privacy" is real in a kind of mundane sense, in that you can't have my headache for me and I can't have your toothache. But that's not a deep metaphysical barrier. It's just a fact about how experiences are individuated, in the same way that you can't take my walk for me.

And I think this becomes really important when we turn to AI, actually, because the temptation is to ask "but does the language model really have the inner red, the private thing?", as if there's a fact of the matter hidden behind the behaviour that we're locked out of. And I want to say, in a sense, that question is malformed. What we have to do instead is look at the whole form of life, if you like. How does this thing engage with the world, with a body or without one, how is it embedded in our practices, what would it even mean for it to be in pain or to see red. Those are hard questions, but they're the right questions. Hunting for the beetle is not.

r001.rationale: The response says that people communicate about red through shared use of the word, such as pointing to the same tomato, responding to traffic lights, and matching paint chips; this shared public practice is what the word needs to do.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we need to distinguish the public circumstances in which we talk about seeing red from the experience itself. We can both point to a tomato, call it red, distinguish it from something green, and agree about whether the lighting is misleading. That gives us a shared practice in which the word “red” has a role.

But I don’t have access to your experience in the way that you do, and you don’t have access to mine. So there’s a temptation to ask, “Yes, but are you really having the same experience as me?” And then we imagine that we each have a private sample that we could somehow bring out and compare. But there isn’t such a comparison available to us.

That doesn’t mean there’s no experience, or that experience is just behaviour. It means we should be careful about the picture of privacy we’re working with. Our language for describing experience is shared, even though the experience we’re describing is our own.

r001.rationale: The response identifies shared public practices around red—pointing to a tomato, naming it red, distinguishing it from green, and discussing misleading lighting—as what people can communicate successfully.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think we have to distinguish between the public circumstances in which we learn to use the word “red” and what we’re tempted to think of as a private object that the word names. We learn colour words through shared activities: pointing to things, sorting them, correcting one another. That gives us a public basis for saying that we both see red.

But then we’re inclined to ask, “Yes, but is your experience of red really the same as mine?” And it’s worth pausing over what would count as answering that question. We can compare what we say, what we distinguish, and how we respond. We can’t put our experiences next to one another in the way we can put two colour samples next to one another.

That doesn’t mean there’s no experience, or that experience is just behaviour. It means we should be careful about assuming that the language of comparing public objects transfers straightforwardly to this supposedly private realm.

r001.rationale: The response says shared practices and comparisons of what people say, distinguish, and how they respond provide a public basis for saying that both see red.
